title: A House of Dynamite
synopsis: An ICBM has been launched from somewhere — they don't know where yet — at the United States. You are the Deputy National Security Adviser. You have eighteen minutes before you have to advise.

nodes.text: Watch Officer's voice loses its shape: single SBIRS detection, ballistic, transpacific, boost phase confirmed. Your coffee goes back down on the ring it made an hour ago. Somebody starts the clock on the big wall and it does not count up. Eighteen minutes. In that time you will advise a man on whether to end a country. Your hands are steady. That will not last.

choices.text: Call STRATCOM first
choices.consequence: You want the number before you face the man. STRATCOM picks up on the second ring, and you buy yourself ninety seconds of being wrong in private.

choices.text: Wake the President first
choices.consequence: You skip confirmation and go straight to the only phone that matters. Whatever comes next, he heard it from you first — right, or catastrophically not.

nodes.text: STRATCOM has it too. Real, depressed trajectory, single warhead by mass estimate, apogee lower than anything in the playbook. Origin box: a stretch of the Sea of Okhotsk the size of Ohio, gray water and nobody's flag. The general says 'we're not assigning that yet' in the voice of a man who has assigned it and won't say so. The wall clock does not care what he won't say.

choices.text: Demand a confidence interval
choices.consequence: You ask for a number with error bars, because numbers are the only thing in this room that can't be intimidated. He gives you one you don't like.

choices.text: Order a second sensor handoff
choices.consequence: You push the track onto a second constellation. Two sensors that hate each other agreeing is worth more than any general's certainty.

nodes.text: Ninety seconds and he's on, and he sounds awake the way certain men are awake at four in the morning — instantly, completely, without any of it reaching the voice. 'Talk to me.' Behind him a door closes. Someone is moving his family. You have not told him the number yet and he has not asked, which tells you he already knows there is one.

choices.text: Brief plainly with what you know
choices.consequence: You give him the raw four sentences and nothing to hide behind. He says thank you, and you hear him write something down.

choices.text: Brief carefully with caveats
choices.consequence: Every qualifier you attach buys him room and costs him seconds. By the third 'preliminary' you can hear him stop listening.

nodes.text: Eighty-seven percent real, and climbing a point every ninety seconds. The origin ellipse has shrunk to something you could drive across. Three candidate countries inside it. Two have arsenals and doctrine and a phone number you know by heart. The third has none of that, which is the possibility nobody here wants to say out loud, because it means the map is wrong.

choices.text: Insist on confirmed attribution before recommendation
choices.consequence: You refuse to name a country on a guess, and the room resents you for it. Thirteen minutes is not long enough to be this careful. You are anyway.

choices.text: Begin contingency planning for all three
choices.consequence: Three folders open at once, three sets of targeting assumptions in the air. Somebody will call this prudence later. Tonight it feels like betting every horse.

nodes.text: Your counterpart in Beijing picks up on the third ring — the channel you spent four years and one humiliating dinner building. He is also at four in the morning. He is also not surprised, which is its own information. 'Not us,' he says. 'Verify.' Then, softer, off the script you both memorized: 'Verify fast.' You write the two words on your palm because your notebook is across the room.

choices.text: Trust the channel and move on
choices.consequence: You spend four years of built credibility in one sentence to the room: it isn't China. Nobody argues. That worries you more than argument would.

choices.text: Press him for one piece of corroborating data
choices.consequence: You ask for a radar cut he is not permitted to give you. The pause on the line runs nine seconds. Then he gives you a bearing and hangs up.

nodes.text: Fort Greely and Vandenberg report ready. Forty-four interceptors in the ground and a Pacific window that closes in under four minutes. The physics is a bullet hitting a bullet, and the honest number for that, which nobody says on camera, sits near a coin flip. Better track means better odds. Better track also means fewer shots. Somebody has to pick, and everyone is looking at the same chair.

choices.text: Authorize the interceptor shot now
choices.consequence: You take the first shot early because early means a second one exists. The launch officer repeats your words back verbatim, which is how you learn your voice is shaking.

choices.text: Hold for better track
choices.consequence: You trade a shot for accuracy and watch the window narrow by a third. If this is wrong you will have thirty years to describe the reasoning.

nodes.text: An Air Force colonel says the word 'consultative' twice, and means it as a warning: the President has authorized discussion, not election. Nothing released. Nothing committed. The distinction is real in doctrine and paper-thin at this speed, and every officer here knows the difference between a legal state and a practical one. The clock has taken eight minutes and given nothing back.

choices.text: Get the President on with the war cabinet now
choices.consequence: You put fourteen faces on the screens at once and fill the room with people who each want a different war. He listens to all of them. It costs ninety seconds.

choices.text: Hold the war cabinet — let him think one more minute
choices.consequence: You give a man sixty seconds of silence in the worst hour of his life. Later you will not know whether that was mercy or malpractice.

nodes.text: The kill vehicle goes. The screen updates every two seconds and the room updates with it, breath by breath. Possible. Possible. Then a technician says 'assess miss' in the tone he'd use to read a lunch order, and the number in the corner keeps counting toward a coast. Somebody's chair squeaks. It is the loudest thing in the building. Two shots left, and after that, arithmetic ends.

choices.text: Authorize second shot
choices.consequence: You call it before the miss finishes rendering. Nobody wants to be the person who waited, and tonight that instinct happens to be correct.

choices.text: Hold for the final shot
choices.consequence: You keep one interceptor back like a card in a bad hand. The colonel's jaw moves. He says nothing, which is worse.

nodes.text: Attribution lands the way it always does — two agencies that dislike each other arriving at the same sentence within a minute. A rogue battery. North Korean uniforms, North Korean hardware, no order from Pyongyang that anyone can find. And on a back channel nobody has used since 2019, the leadership is asking what is happening. They are asking you. Either that question is honest, or it is the most expensive lie ever told.

choices.text: Open the back channel directly
choices.consequence: You pick up a line that has been dead six years, and the man on the other end is breathing like he ran to reach it.

choices.text: Treat the launch as state action until proven otherwise
choices.consequence: You choose the assumption that kills more people if you're wrong, because it kills fewer if you're right. The room writes it down.

nodes.text: Second interceptor: assess miss. Nobody says the word twice this time. The President is on the line, and he does not ask for options or estimates or the nineteen-page annex somebody flew in from Omaha. He asks for one thing he can put in a sentence, because whatever you say next he will still be saying at eighty years old, in a chair, to a grandchild.

choices.text: Tell him: no retaliatory launch, no matter what
choices.consequence: You say it flat, no hedge, no annex: nothing goes back tonight. Three men at the table inhale to object and none of them finishes the breath.

choices.text: Tell him: hold response posture, but reassure allies
choices.consequence: You give him the middle path — hands off the keys, phones to Tokyo and Seoul. It keeps the most doors open and closes none of them cleanly.

nodes.text: The channel is dead air for ninety seconds. Then a North Korean general, three ranks below anyone who should be doing this, confirms it in bad English and worse control of his voice. The battery commander is being dealt with — he uses that phrase. He asks you not to answer. He is frightened in a way that cannot be performed at this hour, and you are the only person alive who has heard it.

choices.text: Trust him on the call alone
choices.consequence: You stake a continent on a stranger's shaking voice with no corroboration whatsoever. It is the least defensible call of your career and you make it in four seconds.

choices.text: Demand a verifiable action in 60 seconds
choices.consequence: You ask him to stand down a second battery where your satellites can watch. He says he lacks the authority. Forty seconds later it happens anyway.

nodes.text: Third interceptor. The screen holds, and holds, and then the track simply stops existing — the cleanest thing you will ever watch a computer do. Somewhere over open Pacific, at an altitude with no name in common speech, it is finished. The room makes a sound that isn't cheering. Then a voice from the back says 'debris field,' and everyone remembers there is an after.

choices.text: Order a public, calm statement immediately
choices.consequence: You get ahead of the phone video some fisherman is already uploading. Forty minutes of calm now buys a decade of not being called liars.

choices.text: Hold all statements for the next hour
choices.consequence: You choose silence and let the rumor build. Right for the intelligence, wrong for everyone watching a strange light over the water.

nodes.text: Third interceptor: miss. Terminal phase. Then the track solution refines, and refines again, and the number that falls out is so improbable the analyst reads it twice before he'll say it: open ocean, three hundred miles west of Mendocino. No landfall. A weapon built to erase a city is going to boil a piece of empty sea. Twenty seconds. Nineteen. You do not yet know whether that is luck or a message.

choices.text: Brace the rooms for the message
choices.consequence: You warn every station in the building what a flash on the horizon looks like through a coastal camera. Some of them thank you. One of them starts crying.

choices.text: Order DEFCON 2 immediately
choices.consequence: You raise the posture on a night that just ended without a city dying, and half the planet's warning systems light up in answer. Escalation is a language, and you shouted.

nodes.text: The clock rolls to zero and past it, and time starts behaving normally again, which nobody here is ready for. The President is still on the line. He looks — on the screen, in a bunker corridor, tie undone — at you. He has been doing that all night, at every branch, when there was nobody else in the world to look at.

choices.text: Recommend public reassurance and quiet diplomacy
choices.consequence: You argue for a small voice and a long game, and you watch two four-star officers decide, permanently, what they think of you.

choices.text: Recommend a measured demonstration of resolve
choices.consequence: You recommend moving a carrier group somewhere cameras can count it. Deterrence is theater, and tonight the audience is everyone.

nodes.text: Zero comes and goes. Somebody opens a window because the air handling can't keep up with forty terrified people. In eighteen minutes you have done the largest thing you will ever do, and the only physical evidence is a legal pad covered in handwriting you don't recognize as yours. Your hands start shaking now, on schedule, late. You put them under the table.

choices.text: Stay in the room for the next twelve hours
choices.consequence: You don't leave, don't eat, and by noon you're the only person who has read every cable in order. That turns out to matter.

choices.text: Hand off to the senior team and rest
choices.consequence: You brief your deputy for nine minutes and go home. You sleep forty of them and wake with the wall clock still running behind your eyes.

nodes.text: He speaks at seven in the morning. The words are yours, drafted on a legal pad and typed by a staffer who cried twice doing it, and against every instinct in the building they are calm and exact and contain no adjectives at all. The country listens. Over the years it will retell this night slightly wrong, and the wrongness will be the kind that helps.

choices.text: Stay in office for the rebuild
choices.consequence: You stay, and the staying costs you a marriage's worth of evenings. The building needs somebody who was in the chair, and you are the only one left.

choices.text: Resign in a year, on your own terms
choices.consequence: You put a date on a calendar twelve months out and tell nobody. Knowing the exit exists is the only thing that lets you keep walking in.

nodes.text: The country survives. The agencies do not all behave well in the after. Three inquiries open, two of them built to find a person rather than a fault, and one senator learns to say your name the way other people say a slur. You testify. You correct the record across four hearings and lose two friendships doing it. A second long night, stretched thin over a year.

choices.text: Push for non-proliferation reforms
choices.consequence: You decide the fight is worth more than the friendships and start writing memos nobody asked for. One of them ends up in a hearing room.

choices.text: Speak at the memorial when the year turns
choices.consequence: You accept an invitation you've been declining for months, then spend three weeks failing to write two minutes.

nodes.text: Sun on the South Lawn, coffee gone cold in a mug stenciled for a trip that never happened. He asks you for a paragraph — one paragraph he can build a year of policy on. You start writing and understand halfway through the second sentence that you are choosing, right here, whether you're the person who stayed or the person who got out clean.

choices.text: Draft the paragraph for a long policy season
choices.consequence: You write it so it can survive a committee, which means you have signed up for every committee. One sentence, and it commits you to a decade.

choices.text: Draft the paragraph for a clean handoff
choices.consequence: You write something a successor could deliver without you in the room. He notices. He reads it anyway, and doesn't ask why.

nodes.text: Under the lights you argue the hardest thing to argue: that the system worked, and that working once is not the same as being safe. The committee leans forward, which is rarer than the cameras suggest. You have exactly one reservoir of credibility from that night and it will fund one fight, not two. You pick in the four seconds before the chairman recognizes you.

choices.text: Spend it on weapons
choices.consequence: You go after the arsenals themselves, the unglamorous arithmetic of fewer objects that can end a city. Progress measured in decades, and you know it going in.

choices.text: Spend it on the warning architecture
choices.consequence: You choose the sensors and the seconds instead — the plumbing nobody names a building after. It will save people who never learn they were saved.

nodes.text: A year on, twenty folding chairs at the Navy Yard for the analysts who sat at consoles that night and did not get to leave the room. Somebody's mother brought sheet cake. You speak for two minutes. Driving home you understand that one of those minutes — the one you didn't write down — is what the rest of your career is supposed to sound like.

choices.text: Turn the speech into a policy push
choices.consequence: You turn two minutes of eulogy into a working group, a white paper, and a mailing list of four hundred people who were also awake that night.

choices.text: Turn the speech into your private vow
choices.consequence: You never publish it. The page goes in a drawer and you read it on the bad mornings, which is a different kind of usefulness.

nodes.text: Two years on, a room in Geneva with bad acoustics and a table too long for the number of people at it. The treaty you sign is partial, unenforceable in three places, and better than what existed the morning before. You are old now, in the way that particular night aged people. You sleep most nights. The dream still comes, but it comes less, and it no longer wakes the house.

You leave on the date you picked and teach at a state school with a name you can pronounce and a parking lot you can see from your office. Your students know that night from a documentary with dramatic music. They don't know you were in the room. You teach them the lessons and withhold the story, and the lessons take, which was the whole point. So, eventually, do you.

The reforms take nine years and slow the next escalation by an amount nobody can measure and everybody argues about. Slow is not stopped. You end up more cynical and more hopeful at once, which sounded like a contradiction at thirty and now just sounds like an accurate description of the work. Somebody else's phone rings at four in the morning. It rings later than it would have.

You spend twenty years on sensors, handoffs, and the ninety seconds between a detection and a human being told about it. The architecture that woke you will, eventually, wake fewer people, and wake them holding better numbers. You'll be retired before it goes live. Someone in a room you will never see gets eight extra minutes and never learns your name. That is the correct shape of a legacy.
